results.comment: From a former US Navy Recruiter:  To get a Navy Challenge contract (SEALs, EOD, SWCC, Navy Diver), you need to do at least 75 push-ups and 75 sit-ups. Most SOF guys will tell you that you aren't really competitive unless you can do at least 100 of each. You actually failed the pull-ups section of the test because you need to perform the pull-up with your hands facing away. Challenge PST observers would have scored you both zero on your pull-ups. To get a Challenge contract a person needs to do 15 pull-ups. I'm sure you both know you need to work on running and swimming, but a Challenge contract requires times of less than 9:30 in each. Also, don't swim with shoes on. To actually get through BUD/S, SEALs recommend that you show up being able to swim 500 yards in under 8:00, at least 100 push-ups and sit-ups, at least 20 pull-ups, and be able to run 1.5 miles in less than 8:00. Once you hit those numbers, focus on running longer distances and doing swim workouts with fins. Fins do make you go faster, but if you swim for the same time in fins, until you're used to them, your calves will be on fire. According to Stew Smith who studies the physical statistics of those who make it through BUD/S, the better you are at running, the more likely you are to make it through BUD/S.
results.comment_focus_summary: Advice about required physical standards (push-ups, sit-ups, pull-ups, run and swim times) for getting a Navy Challenge/BUD/S contract and common mistakes (pull-up form, swimming with shoes, using fins).

results.comment: Hey guys, I’ve taken about 7 or 8 PSTs in the last year, passed all of them and received a Navy rescue swimmer contract. So here is my $.2. This is just for anyone wondering, not to be a YouTube troll. Good on you guys for trying. These are called PST(physical screening test) and are done by all spec op/war candidates to earn a contract.   Swim- in my opinion the swim always warmed up my shoulders and body in general. Going cold into push ups and pull ups is rough. Also, I don’t remember if Seals can do breast stroke, but they mostly use combat side stroke. Rescue swimmers have to do freestyle. You guys did some sort breast stroke thing. Breast stroke is a great stroke and relaxing, but not the fastest. The major difference is that you’re doing it in a pool and can push off the walls which helps a lot. It also helps keep you in a straight line. If you zigzag around, you just swim more. You also had 10 minutes to change and with demonstrations probably a 15 minute rest after the swim.   Pushups- solid form, def keep your eyes up. PRO TIP: sort of twisting your hand into the ground will turn your elbows closer/into your torso and facing more directly behind you. Forearm facing toward. In turn you will use the bigger muscles in your chest and overtime will be able to get really good numbers. When your elbows are bowed out in the down position you use a lot of shoulder and no matter what will tire out faster. 60 ish push ups mostly as far as you will get with your elbows out. To get those 80-100 numbers get that elbow in.   Sit ups- arms across chest and hands on the collar bones. Over the knee was definitely extra. We did maybe 2 Inches below the knee.   Pull ups- hands forward. Aside from that, they were solid looking.   Run- 10:50 isn’t a bad time. 10:15 was auto qual for RS. Not sure about SO.   If you guys are ever in San Diego, ca let me know if you want to do something on base. Cheers.
